items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A strong chemical bond formed when two atoms share a pair of electrons"?
items.answer: covalent bond
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of covalent bond.

items.stem: Which molecule is NOT a polymer?
items.answer: glucose
items.markingKey: C. Glucose is a monosaccharide monomer.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain the relationship between condensation and hydrolysis reactions in metabolism.
items.answer: Condensation (anabolism) joins monomers into polymers with release of water, e.g. glucose → glycogen for storage; hydrolysis (catabolism) breaks polymers into monomers using water, e.g. digestion of starch; they are reverse reactions catalysed by different enzymes. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Condensation (anabolism) joins monomers into polymers with release of water, e.g. glucose → glycogen for storage; hydrolysis (catabolism) breaks polymers into monomers using water, e.g. digestion of starch; they are reverse reactions catalysed by different enzymes. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
The table shows the number of carbon atoms, the number of cis C=C double bonds and the melting point of some fatty acids.

Fatty acid | Carbon atoms | C=C double bonds | Melting point / °C
myristic acid | 14 | 0 | 54.4
palmitic acid | 16 | 0 | 62.9
stearic acid | 18 | 0 | 69.3
oleic acid | 18 | 1 | 13.4
linoleic acid | 18 | 2 | -5.0
α-linolenic acid | 18 | 3 | -11.0

(a) State the melting point of oleic acid. [1]
(b) Describe the effect of chain length on the melting point of saturated fatty acids. [2]
items.answer: (a) 13.4 °C (b) Melting point increases with chain length, by about 7.4 °C per two extra carbons.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 13.4 °C (A1). (b) [2] Positive relationship (A1); quantified using data (A1).

items.stem: A polysaccharide of 500 glucose units is completely hydrolysed. How many water molecules are used?
items.markingKey: A. One water per glycosidic bond broken.

items.stem:
Glucose solutions of known concentration were heated with excess Benedict’s reagent for 5 minutes. The brick-red precipitate was filtered off and the percentage transmission of red light through the remaining blue filtrate was measured with a colorimeter.

Glucose concentration / mol dm⁻³ | Transmission / %
0.0 | 13
0.2 | 39
0.4 | 56
0.6 | 69
0.8 | 77
1.0 | 83

A sample of orange juice, treated the same way, gave 47 % transmission.

(a) Describe the relationship between glucose concentration and transmission. [2]
(b) Estimate the glucose concentration of the sample (orange juice) by interpolation. [2]
(c) Calculate the percentage change in transmission between 0.2 and 1.0 mol dm⁻³. [2]
items.answer: (a) As glucose concentration increases, transmission increases; the increase is not linear and becomes smaller at higher concentrations. (b) about 0.29 mol dm⁻³ (c) +112.8 %
items.markingKey: (a) [2] Positive relationship (A1); non-linear / levels off (A1). (b) [2] Interpolation between the bracketing standards (M1); ≈ 0.29 mol dm⁻³, accept ±0.05 (A1). (c) [2] (83 − 39)/39 × 100 (M1) = +112.8 % (A1).

items.stem: Which bond links monosaccharides in a disaccharide?
items.answer: glycosidic bond
items.markingKey: C. Formed by condensation between –OH groups.

items.stem: Rafael writes: "Hydrolysis releases water as large molecules are broken down." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Hydrolysis uses (consumes) water to break bonds; it is condensation that releases water.
items.markingKey: Hydrolysis uses (consumes) water to break bonds; it is condensation that releases water. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between condensation and hydrolysis.
items.answer: Condensation joins two molecules by a covalent bond and releases water (building polymers); hydrolysis breaks a covalent bond by adding water (breaking polymers into monomers).
items.markingKey: Condensation joins two molecules by a covalent bond and releases water (building polymers); hydrolysis breaks a covalent bond by adding water (breaking polymers into monomers). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which the synthesis of glycogen in liver cells after a meal shows condensation reactions.
items.answer: Glucose units are linked by condensation into branched glycogen molecules for storage. Each new glycosidic bond formed releases a molecule of water, building a polymer from monomers.
items.markingKey: Context (Glucose units are linked by condensation into branched glycogen molecules for storage.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Each new glycosidic bond formed releases a molecule of water, building a polymer from monomers. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to condensation reactions.

items.stem: Explain how condensation and hydrolysis reactions are involved in building and breaking down carbohydrates, proteins and lipids.
items.answer: Condensation: glucose → disaccharide/polysaccharide (glycosidic bonds); amino acids → polypeptides (peptide bonds); glycerol + 3 fatty acids → triglyceride (ester bonds); water released; energy required. Hydrolysis: reverse, water added, digestive enzymes (amylase, protease, lipase), releases monomers.
items.markingKey: Condensation: glucose → disaccharide/polysaccharide (glycosidic bonds); amino acids → polypeptides (peptide bonds); glycerol + 3 fatty acids → triglyceride (ester bonds); water released; energy required. Hydrolysis: reverse, water added, digestive enzymes (amylase, protease, lipase), releases monomers.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "cellulose".
items.answer: An unbranched polysaccharide of β-glucose in which alternate units are inverted, forming straight chains that bundle into microfibrils
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: an unbranched polysaccharide of β-glucose in which alternate units are inverted, forming straight chains that bundle into microfibrils. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain how the structure of starch makes it a suitable energy store in plants.
items.answer: Starch is a large, insoluble polymer so it does not affect water potential; amylose is compact (helical) so much glucose is stored in small space; amylopectin is branched for faster hydrolysis; glucose is easily released by hydrolysis for respiration.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Starch is a large, insoluble polymer so it does not affect water potential; amylose is compact (helical) so much glucose is stored in small space; amylopectin is branched for faster hydrolysis; glucose is easily released by hydrolysis for respiration. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Why is glucose not stored in cells as free glucose?
options: It is too large to stay in cells.
It is soluble and would lower the water potential, causing osmotic water uptake.
items.answer: It is soluble and would lower the water potential, causing osmotic water uptake.
items.markingKey: D. Polysaccharides are insoluble and osmotically inactive.

items.stem: "Glycogen is stored in plants and starch in animals." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Glycogen is the storage polysaccharide in animals and fungi; starch is the storage polysaccharide in plants.
items.markingKey: Glycogen is the storage polysaccharide in animals and fungi; starch is the storage polysaccharide in plants. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Draw the ring structures of α-glucose and β-glucose and describe the difference your drawings should show.
items.answer: Hexagonal rings with five carbons and one oxygen, carbon 6 above the ring; in α-glucose the OH on C1 is below the ring, in β-glucose above.
items.markingKey: Hexagonal rings with five carbons and one oxygen, carbon 6 above the ring; in α-glucose the OH on C1 is below the ring, in β-glucose above.

items.stem: A food sample gives a blue-black colour with iodine and no change with Benedict’s reagent. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Neither starch nor sugar is present.
Starch is present but no reducing sugar.
items.answer: Starch is present but no reducing sugar.
items.markingKey: D. Iodine detects starch; Benedict’s detects reducing sugars.

items.stem: Compare the structure and functions of starch, glycogen and cellulose.
items.answer: Monomers: α-glucose (starch, glycogen) vs β-glucose (cellulose). Bonds: α-1,4 and α-1,6 vs β-1,4. Branching: amylose none/helix, amylopectin some, glycogen highly branched, cellulose straight chains with H bonds → microfibrils. Functions: energy storage in plants/animals, structural support in cell walls. Insoluble – no osmotic effect.
items.markingKey: Monomers: α-glucose (starch, glycogen) vs β-glucose (cellulose). Bonds: α-1,4 and α-1,6 vs β-1,4. Branching: amylose none/helix, amylopectin some, glycogen highly branched, cellulose straight chains with H bonds → microfibrils. Functions: energy storage in plants/animals, structural support in cell walls. Insoluble – no osmotic effect.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Starch is a better energy store than glycogen."
items.answer: Neither is better in absolute terms; each is adapted to the metabolic demands of the organisms that use it.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: amylose is very compact due to helical coiling, storing much glucose in little space; plants have low metabolic rates, so slow release is sufficient. Arguments against: glycogen’s extensive branching releases glucose faster, suiting active animals; each is suited to the organism’s needs rather than one being better. Supported judgement: Neither is better in absolute terms; each is adapted to the metabolic demands of the organisms that use it. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A single sugar unit such as glucose, fructose or galactose, the monomer of carbohydrates"?
items.answer: monosaccharide
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of monosaccharide.

items.stem: Explain why glycogen is suited to energy storage in animals.
items.answer: It is insoluble and compact; it is very highly branched with many ends, so enzymes can hydrolyse it rapidly to supply glucose for the high metabolic demands of animals.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It is insoluble and compact; it is very highly branched with many ends, so enzymes can hydrolyse it rapidly to supply glucose for the high metabolic demands of animals. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between β-glucose and α-glucose.
items.answer: In α-glucose the –OH on carbon 1 is below the ring; in β-glucose it is above; α-glucose polymerises into starch and glycogen, β-glucose into cellulose.
items.markingKey: In α-glucose the –OH on carbon 1 is below the ring; in β-glucose it is above; α-glucose polymerises into starch and glycogen, β-glucose into cellulose. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which cotton fibres used in textiles shows the structure–function relationship of cellulose.
items.answer: Cotton fibres are about 90 % cellulose and are very strong and absorbent. Parallel β-glucose chains hydrogen-bonded into microfibrils give high tensile strength; free –OH groups make the fibres absorbent.
items.markingKey: Context (Cotton fibres are about 90 % cellulose and are very strong and absorbent.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Parallel β-glucose chains hydrogen-bonded into microfibrils give high tensile strength; free –OH groups make the fibres absorbent. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the structure–function relationship of cellulose.

items.stem: A student claims: "Starch and cellulose are both made of β-glucose." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Starch is made of α-glucose; cellulose is made of β-glucose.
items.markingKey: Starch is made of α-glucose; cellulose is made of β-glucose. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

(a) Describe the relationship between glucose concentration and transmission. [2]
(b) Estimate the glucose concentration of the sample (coconut water) by interpolation. [2]
(c) Calculate the percentage change in transmission between 0.2 and 1.0 mol dm⁻³. [2]
items.answer: (a) As glucose concentration increases, transmission increases; the increase is not linear and becomes smaller at higher concentrations. (b) about 0.78 mol dm⁻³ (c) +125.0 %

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "cell recognition"?
options: A reaction in which a covalent bond between two monomers is broken by the addition of a molecule of water
The ability of cells to identify other cells, e.g. as self or non-self, using molecules such as glycoproteins on the cell surface
An unbranched polysaccharide of β-glucose in which alternate units are inverted, forming straight chains that bundle into microfibrils
A single sugar unit such as glucose, fructose or galactose, the monomer of carbohydrates
items.answer: The ability of cells to identify other cells, e.g. as self or non-self, using molecules such as glycoproteins on the cell surface
items.markingKey: B. "cell recognition" is the ability of cells to identify other cells, e.g. as self or non-self, using molecules such as glycoproteins on the cell surface.

items.stem: Explain the difference between glycoproteins and glycolipids.
items.answer: Glycoproteins are proteins with attached carbohydrate chains; glycolipids are lipids with attached carbohydrate chains; both contribute to the glycocalyx and cell recognition.
items.markingKey: Glycoproteins are proteins with attached carbohydrate chains; glycolipids are lipids with attached carbohydrate chains; both contribute to the glycocalyx and cell recognition. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why can glycoproteins act as recognition molecules?
options: They are found inside the nucleus.
The carbohydrate chains are very varied and have specific shapes.
items.answer: The carbohydrate chains are very varied and have specific shapes.
items.markingKey: D. Diversity of sugar sequences gives specificity.

items.stem: With reference to ABO blood typing before transfusion in hospitals, explain how it illustrates cell recognition by glycoproteins.
items.answer: Samples are mixed with anti-A and anti-B sera; agglutination shows which antigens are present. Antibodies recognise specific carbohydrate antigens on red cells, so mismatched transfusion leads to agglutination and haemolysis.
items.markingKey: Context (Samples are mixed with anti-A and anti-B sera; agglutination shows which antigens are present.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Antibodies recognise specific carbohydrate antigens on red cells, so mismatched transfusion leads to agglutination and haemolysis. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to cell recognition by glycoproteins.

items.stem: Arjun writes: "Blood group O has O antigens that are recognised by all antibodies." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Group O red cells lack both A and B antigens (they carry only the unmodified H chain), so anti-A and anti-B do not react with them.
items.markingKey: Group O red cells lack both A and B antigens (they carry only the unmodified H chain), so anti-A and anti-B do not react with them. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the role of glycoproteins in cell recognition, using the ABO blood group system as an example.
items.answer: Glycoproteins: protein + carbohydrate, extracellular, glycocalyx; diverse sugar chains = markers; ABO: H chain; IA adds N-acetylgalactosamine, IB galactose; O none; antibodies against absent antigens; agglutination; transfusion compatibility; other roles: sperm–egg recognition, immune self/non-self, hormone receptors.
items.markingKey: Glycoproteins: protein + carbohydrate, extracellular, glycocalyx; diverse sugar chains = markers; ABO: H chain; IA adds N-acetylgalactosamine, IB galactose; O none; antibodies against absent antigens; agglutination; transfusion compatibility; other roles: sperm–egg recognition, immune self/non-self, hormone receptors.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A protein with carbohydrate chains attached, often found in the plasma membrane with the carbohydrate facing outwards"?
items.answer: glycoprotein
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of glycoprotein.

items.stem: Explain the basis of the ABO blood group system.
items.answer: Red blood cells carry glycoproteins with a carbohydrate chain (O/H antigen); allele IA adds a sugar making antigen A, IB adds a different sugar making antigen B, i lacks the enzyme; antibodies in plasma react with antigens not present on own cells, causing agglutination in incompatible transfusions.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Red blood cells carry glycoproteins with a carbohydrate chain (O/H antigen); allele IA adds a sugar making antigen A, IB adds a different sugar making antigen B, i lacks the enzyme; antibodies in plasma react with antigens not present on own cells, causing agglutination in incompatible transfusions. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Rafael’s blood sample shows no agglutination with anti-A serum and agglutination with anti-B serum. Deduce Rafael’s blood group, state which antibodies are in the plasma, and identify which donor groups of red cells could be given.
items.answer: Group B; plasma antibodies: anti-A; compatible donors: B, O
items.markingKey: Group B from agglutination pattern (A1); antibodies against antigens absent from own cells (A1); donors whose cells lack antigens recognised by recipient plasma: B, O (A1).

items.stem: A patient’s red cells agglutinate with anti-B serum but not with anti-A serum. What is the patient’s blood group?
items.answer: B
items.markingKey: B. Reaction with anti-B only = B antigen only.

items.stem: "Blood group O donors should always be used in emergencies." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: O negative red cells are appropriate in emergencies, but group-specific blood should be used as soon as the recipient’s group is known.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: O red cells lack A and B antigens, so they are compatible with all ABO recipients; it saves time when the recipient’s group is unknown. Arguments against: O plasma contains anti-A and anti-B, so plasma products are not universal; O supplies are limited and Rh status must also be considered (O negative). Supported judgement: O negative red cells are appropriate in emergencies, but group-specific blood should be used as soon as the recipient’s group is known. Markbands (8 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "steroid"?
options: A lipid with a structure of four fused carbon rings, such as cholesterol, oestradiol and testosterone
The form of glucose in which the –OH on carbon 1 is below the plane of the ring
An unbranched polysaccharide of β-glucose in which alternate units are inverted, forming straight chains that bundle into microfibrils
A lipid with a glycerol bonded to two fatty acids and a phosphate group, giving a hydrophilic head and two hydrophobic tails
items.answer: A lipid with a structure of four fused carbon rings, such as cholesterol, oestradiol and testosterone
items.markingKey: A. "steroid" is a lipid with a structure of four fused carbon rings, such as cholesterol, oestradiol and testosterone.

items.stem: Explain how the structure of a phospholipid allows the formation of a membrane.
items.answer: A phospholipid has a hydrophilic phosphate head and two hydrophobic fatty-acid tails (amphipathic); in water the heads face the aqueous surroundings and the tails face inward, forming a bilayer that is a barrier to polar substances.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A phospholipid has a hydrophilic phosphate head and two hydrophobic fatty-acid tails (amphipathic); in water the heads face the aqueous surroundings and the tails face inward, forming a bilayer that is a barrier to polar substances. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Why can steroid hormones pass directly through the plasma membrane?
options: They are very large polar molecules.
They are carried by channel proteins.
They are lipids, so they dissolve in the hydrophobic core of the bilayer.
items.answer: They are lipids, so they dissolve in the hydrophobic core of the bilayer.
items.markingKey: D. Then they bind intracellular receptors.

items.stem: A student claims: "Lipids are only bad for health." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Lipids are essential: energy stores, membranes (phospholipids, cholesterol), insulation, hormones (steroids); some are linked to disease in excess.
items.markingKey: Lipids are essential: energy stores, membranes (phospholipids, cholesterol), insulation, hormones (steroids); some are linked to disease in excess. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A fatty acid has the formula C13H23COOH. Deduce the number of carbon–carbon double bonds and state whether it is saturated, monounsaturated or polyunsaturated.
items.answer: 2; polyunsaturated
items.markingKey: Saturated formula C13H27COOH (M1); (27 − 23)/2 = 2 double bonds (A1); polyunsaturated (A1).

items.stem: Briefly describe the blubber of harp seals and whales and explain what it reveals about the roles of triglycerides.
items.answer: Blubber can be over 10 cm thick and make up 30–50 % of body mass in some marine mammals. Blubber stores energy for fasting periods and provides thermal insulation in cold water.
items.markingKey: Context (Blubber can be over 10 cm thick and make up 30–50 % of body mass in some marine mammals.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Blubber stores energy for fasting periods and provides thermal insulation in cold water. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the roles of triglycerides.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Lipids are a better energy store than carbohydrates for all organisms."
items.answer: Lipids are better for long-term, compact storage, especially in mobile animals; carbohydrates are better for rapid energy release; organisms use both.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: lipids store about twice as much energy per gram and are stored without water; they are ideal for animals that must move or fly, such as migrating birds. Arguments against: carbohydrates can be mobilised and respired faster and can be used anaerobically; plants, which do not move, often store starch, and seeds use both. Supported judgement: Lipids are better for long-term, compact storage, especially in mobile animals; carbohydrates are better for rapid energy release; organisms use both.

items.stem: Describe the structure of triglycerides and phospholipids and explain how these structures relate to their functions.
items.answer: Triglyceride: glycerol + 3 fatty acids, ester bonds, condensation (3 H₂O), hydrophobic; energy storage (37 kJ/g), insulation, buoyancy. Phospholipid: glycerol + 2 fatty acids + phosphate; amphipathic; bilayer; membranes. Saturated vs unsaturated affects fluidity/melting point. Steroids (cholesterol) in membranes and hormones.
items.markingKey: Triglyceride: glycerol + 3 fatty acids, ester bonds, condensation (3 H₂O), hydrophobic; energy storage (37 kJ/g), insulation, buoyancy. Phospholipid: glycerol + 2 fatty acids + phosphate; amphipathic; bilayer; membranes. Saturated vs unsaturated affects fluidity/melting point. Steroids (cholesterol) in membranes and hormones.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A lipid formed by condensation of one glycerol molecule with three fatty acids, linked by ester bonds"?
items.answer: triglyceride
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of triglyceride.

items.stem: Explain the difference between triglycerides and phospholipids.
items.answer: Triglycerides have three fatty acids on glycerol and are hydrophobic energy stores; phospholipids have two fatty acids and a phosphate group, are amphipathic and form membranes.
items.markingKey: Triglycerides have three fatty acids on glycerol and are hydrophobic energy stores; phospholipids have two fatty acids and a phosphate group, are amphipathic and form membranes. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Nia writes: "Phospholipids are completely hydrophobic." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Phospholipids are amphipathic: a hydrophilic phosphate head and hydrophobic tails.
items.markingKey: Phospholipids are amphipathic: a hydrophilic phosphate head and hydrophobic tails. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A fatty acid has the formula C₁₇H₃₁COOH. How many C=C double bonds does it contain?
items.markingKey: B. Saturated C₁₇H₃₅COOH; each double bond removes 2 H: (35 − 31)/2 = 2 (linoleic acid).

items.stem: A ruby-throated hummingbird before crossing the Gulf of Mexico needs to store 800 kJ of energy. Calculate the mass of triglyceride and the mass of glycogen needed  given that they release 37 kJ g⁻¹ and 17 kJ g⁻¹ respectively. Glycogen is stored with about 2 g of water per gram. Calculate the total stored mass for glycogen and explain the advantage of lipid storage for this animal.
items.answer: triglyceride 21.6 g; glycogen 47.1 g; glycogen + water ≈ 141 g; lipid is about 6.53 times lighter, important for mobility
items.markingKey: 800/37 = 21.6 g (A1); 800/17 = 47.1 g (A1). 47.1 × 3 = 141 g (A1); lipid stored anhydrous, much less mass to carry (R1).

items.stem: Which form of glucose makes up cellulose?
items.answer: β-glucose
items.markingKey: D. β-1,4 bonds with alternate units inverted.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "amphipathic".
items.answer: Describes a molecule that has both hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions, such as a phospholipid
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: describes a molecule that has both hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions, such as a phospholipid. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Define the term "covalent bond".
items.answer: A strong chemical bond formed when two atoms share a pair of electrons
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a strong chemical bond formed when two atoms share a pair of electrons. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between glycolipids and glycoproteins.
items.answer: Glycoproteins are proteins with attached carbohydrate chains; glycolipids are lipids with attached carbohydrate chains; both contribute to the glycocalyx and cell recognition.
items.markingKey: Glycoproteins are proteins with attached carbohydrate chains; glycolipids are lipids with attached carbohydrate chains; both contribute to the glycocalyx and cell recognition. items.stem: Which explains the high tensile strength of cellulose?
options: Straight chains lie parallel and are held by many hydrogen bonds into microfibrils.
Its chains are coiled into helices.
items.answer: Straight chains lie parallel and are held by many hydrogen bonds into microfibrils.
items.markingKey: C. Alternate inverted β-glucose units allow straight chains.

items.stem: Explain the difference between cis fatty acids and trans fatty acids.
items.answer: In cis fatty acids the hydrogens are on the same side of the double bond, causing a bend; in trans fatty acids they are on opposite sides, giving a straighter chain that behaves more like a saturated fat.
items.markingKey: In cis fatty acids the hydrogens are on the same side of the double bond, causing a bend; in trans fatty acids they are on opposite sides, giving a straighter chain that behaves more like a saturated fat. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between anabolism and catabolism.
items.answer: Anabolism builds larger molecules from smaller ones (e.g. by condensation), requiring energy; catabolism breaks larger molecules into smaller ones (e.g. by hydrolysis), often releasing energy.
items.markingKey: Anabolism builds larger molecules from smaller ones (e.g. by condensation), requiring energy; catabolism breaks larger molecules into smaller ones (e.g. by hydrolysis), often releasing energy. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Glycoproteins are found on the inner surface of the plasma membrane." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The carbohydrate parts face outward on the extracellular surface, where they can be recognised.
items.markingKey: The carbohydrate parts face outward on the extracellular surface, where they can be recognised. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between starch and glycogen.
items.answer: Glycogen is the animal storage polysaccharide and is more highly branched; starch (amylose + amylopectin) is the plant storage polysaccharide and is less branched.
items.markingKey: Glycogen is the animal storage polysaccharide and is more highly branched; starch (amylose + amylopectin) is the plant storage polysaccharide and is less branched. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A fatty acid has the formula C11H19COOH. Deduce the number of carbon–carbon double bonds and state whether it is saturated, monounsaturated or polyunsaturated.
items.answer: 2; polyunsaturated
items.markingKey: Saturated formula C11H23COOH (M1); (23 − 19)/2 = 2 double bonds (A1); polyunsaturated (A1).

items.stem: Glucose has the formula C₆H₁₂O₆ (Mr = 180). Deduce the molecular formula and relative molecular mass of an unbranched chain of 10 glucose units.
A patient with blood group A needs a red-cell transfusion. Which donor group would be compatible?
items.answer: O
items.markingKey: B. Group A plasma contains antibodies against B; donor O cells carry neither antigen.

items.stem: Briefly describe cotton fibres used in textiles and explain what it reveals about the structure–function relationship of cellulose.
items.answer: Cotton fibres are about 90 % cellulose and are very strong and absorbent. Parallel β-glucose chains hydrogen-bonded into microfibrils give high tensile strength; free –OH groups make the fibres absorbent.
items.markingKey: Context (Cotton fibres are about 90 % cellulose and are very strong and absorbent.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Parallel β-glucose chains hydrogen-bonded into microfibrils give high tensile strength; free –OH groups make the fibres absorbent. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the structure–function relationship of cellulose.

items.stem: Using the blubber of harp seals and whales as an example, explain the roles of triglycerides.
items.answer: Blubber can be over 10 cm thick and make up 30–50 % of body mass in some marine mammals. Blubber stores energy for fasting periods and provides thermal insulation in cold water.
items.markingKey: Context (Blubber can be over 10 cm thick and make up 30–50 % of body mass in some marine mammals.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Blubber stores energy for fasting periods and provides thermal insulation in cold water. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the roles of triglycerides.

items.stem: "Hydrolysis releases water as large molecules are broken down." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Hydrolysis uses (consumes) water to break bonds; it is condensation that releases water.
items.markingKey: Hydrolysis uses (consumes) water to break bonds; it is condensation that releases water. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Leila’s blood sample shows agglutination with anti-A serum and no agglutination with anti-B serum. Deduce Leila’s blood group, state which antibodies are in the plasma, and identify which donor groups of red cells could be given.
items.answer: Group A; plasma antibodies: anti-B; compatible donors: A, O
items.markingKey: Group A from agglutination pattern (A1); antibodies against antigens absent from own cells (A1); donors whose cells lack antigens recognised by recipient plasma: A, O (A1).

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Starch is a better energy store than glycogen."
items.answer: Neither is better in absolute terms; each is adapted to the metabolic demands of the organisms that use it.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: amylose is very compact due to helical coiling, storing much glucose in little space; plants have low metabolic rates, so slow release is sufficient. Arguments against: glycogen’s extensive branching releases glucose faster, suiting active animals; each is suited to the organism’s needs rather than one being better. Supported judgement: Neither is better in absolute terms; each is adapted to the metabolic demands of the organisms that use it.

items.stem: "Lipids are a better energy store than carbohydrates for all organisms." Discuss.
items.answer: Lipids are better for long-term, compact storage, especially in mobile animals; carbohydrates are better for rapid energy release; organisms use both.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: lipids store about twice as much energy per gram and are stored without water; they are ideal for animals that must move or fly, such as migrating birds. Arguments against: carbohydrates can be mobilised and respired faster and can be used anaerobically; plants, which do not move, often store starch, and seeds use both. Supported judgement: Lipids are better for long-term, compact storage, especially in mobile animals; carbohydrates are better for rapid energy release; organisms use both. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: "Carbon is the only element on which life could be based." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Carbon is far better suited than alternatives such as silicon (whose compounds are less stable and less diverse in water), but with only one known example of life the claim cannot be proven.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: carbon forms four stable covalent bonds and long chains, giving vast molecular diversity; carbon compounds are stable but reactive enough at Earth temperatures. Arguments against: silicon can also form four bonds and chains; we have only one example of life, so other chemistries cannot be ruled out. Supported judgement: Carbon is far better suited than alternatives such as silicon (whose compounds are less stable and less diverse in water), but with only one known example of life the claim cannot be proven. items.stem:
The table shows the number of carbon atoms, the number of cis C=C double bonds and the melting point of some fatty acids.

Fatty acid | Carbon atoms | C=C double bonds | Melting point / °C
myristic acid | 14 | 0 | 54.4
stearic acid | 18 | 0 | 69.3
arachidic acid | 20 | 0 | 75.5
oleic acid | 18 | 1 | 13.4
linoleic acid | 18 | 2 | -5.0
α-linolenic acid | 18 | 3 | -11.0

(a) State the melting point of oleic acid. [1]
(b) Describe the effect of chain length on the melting point of saturated fatty acids. [2]
(c) Calculate the difference in melting point between stearic acid and oleic acid. [1]
(d) Calculate the percentage decrease in melting point from stearic to oleic acid. [2]
(e) Explain the effect of double bonds on melting point. [3]
(f) Predict, with a reason, whether a fat rich in linoleic acid would be solid or liquid at 20 °C. [1]
(g) Suggest why fish living in cold water have more polyunsaturated fatty acids in their membranes. [2]
items.answer: (a) 13.4 °C (b) Melting point increases with chain length, by about 7.0 °C per two extra carbons. (c) 55.9 °C (d) 81 % (e) Cis double bonds put kinks in the chain so molecules cannot pack closely; fewer intermolecular attractions; less energy needed to separate them. (f) Liquid – its melting point (−5 °C) is below 20 °C. (g) Polyunsaturated fatty acids have low melting points, keeping membranes fluid at low temperatures so membrane proteins can function.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 13.4 °C (A1). (b) [2] Positive relationship (A1); quantified using data (A1). (c) [1] 69.3 − 13.4 = 55.9 °C (A1). (d) [2] (69.3 − 13.4)/69.3 × 100 (M1) = 81 % (A1). (e) [3] Kinks / bent chains (A1); looser packing, weaker attractions (A1); lower melting point (A1). (f) [1] Liquid with data-based reason (A1). (g) [2] Low melting point / maintain fluidity (A1); link to membrane function (A1).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "polysaccharide"?
options: A carbohydrate polymer made of many monosaccharides joined by glycosidic bonds, e.g. starch, glycogen and cellulose
A protein with carbohydrate chains attached, often found in the plasma membrane with the carbohydrate facing outwards
A lipid with a structure of four fused carbon rings, such as cholesterol, oestradiol and testosterone
A fatty acid with no carbon–carbon double bonds in its hydrocarbon chain
items.answer: A carbohydrate polymer made of many monosaccharides joined by glycosidic bonds, e.g. starch, glycogen and cellulose
items.markingKey: A. "polysaccharide" is a carbohydrate polymer made of many monosaccharides joined by glycosidic bonds, e.g. starch, glycogen and cellulose.

items.stem: Approximately how much energy does 1 g of lipid release when respired, compared with 1 g of carbohydrate?
options: about twice as much (37 kJ vs 17 kJ)
items.answer: about twice as much (37 kJ vs 17 kJ)
items.markingKey: B. Lipids are more reduced (more C–H bonds).

items.stem: Which reaction type builds polypeptides from amino acids?
items.answer: condensation
items.markingKey: condensation. Each peptide bond releases one water molecule.

items.stem: Explain how glycoproteins are involved in cell recognition.
items.answer: Glycoproteins in the plasma membrane carry carbohydrate chains projecting outwards; the specific sequence and shape of these chains act as markers that are recognised by complementary receptors on other cells or by antibodies, allowing self/non-self recognition and cell–cell adhesion.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Glycoproteins in the plasma membrane carry carbohydrate chains projecting outwards; the specific sequence and shape of these chains act as markers that are recognised by complementary receptors on other cells or by antibodies, allowing self/non-self recognition and cell–cell adhesion. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Why is glycogen more highly branched than amylose?
options: Branches make it a structural molecule.
Branches allow hydrogen bonds between chains.
Branches make glycogen soluble in water.
Many branch ends allow rapid hydrolysis to release glucose when energy is needed.
items.answer: Many branch ends allow rapid hydrolysis to release glucose when energy is needed.
items.markingKey: D. Animals need rapid glucose mobilisation.

items.stem: Why do unsaturated fats tend to be liquid at room temperature?
options: Cis double bonds create kinks that prevent close packing of chains.
They form ester bonds with water.
items.answer: Cis double bonds create kinks that prevent close packing of chains.
items.markingKey: A. Weaker intermolecular forces = lower melting point.

items.stem: Why is energy needed to build polymers by condensation in cells?
options: Forming covalent bonds between monomers is an anabolic process requiring energy, often from ATP.
Polymers are less stable than monomers.
Condensation releases large amounts of energy.
items.answer: Forming covalent bonds between monomers is an anabolic process requiring energy, often from ATP.
items.markingKey: A. Anabolism uses energy; hydrolysis (catabolism) releases it.

items.stem: What happens if group A blood is transfused into a group O recipient?
options: The blood changes to group O.
The donor cells destroy the recipient’s cells.
The recipient’s anti-A antibodies cause agglutination of the donor cells.
items.answer: The recipient’s anti-A antibodies cause agglutination of the donor cells.
items.markingKey: D. O recipients have anti-A and anti-B.

items.stem: A student claims: "Cellulose is a storage carbohydrate in plants." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Cellulose is structural (cell walls); starch is the storage carbohydrate of plants.
items.markingKey: Cellulose is structural (cell walls); starch is the storage carbohydrate of plants. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: An Arctic fox and an emperor penguin both have thick fat layers. Which function of adipose tissue is most important to them in winter?
options: thermal insulation as well as energy storage
items.answer: thermal insulation as well as energy storage
items.markingKey: D. Fat (blubber) insulates and stores energy.

items.stem: How many water molecules are released when 12 glucose molecules are joined into an unbranched chain?
items.markingKey: D. n − 1 bonds for a chain of n monomers.

items.stem: Outline one way in which ABO blood typing before transfusion in hospitals shows cell recognition by glycoproteins.
items.answer: Samples are mixed with anti-A and anti-B sera; agglutination shows which antigens are present. Antibodies recognise specific carbohydrate antigens on red cells, so mismatched transfusion leads to agglutination and haemolysis.
items.markingKey: Context (Samples are mixed with anti-A and anti-B sera; agglutination shows which antigens are present.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Antibodies recognise specific carbohydrate antigens on red cells, so mismatched transfusion leads to agglutination and haemolysis. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to cell recognition by glycoproteins.

items.stem:
Glucose solutions of known concentration were heated with excess Benedict’s reagent for 5 minutes. The brick-red precipitate was filtered off and the percentage transmission of red light through the remaining blue filtrate was measured with a colorimeter.

Glucose concentration / mol dm⁻³ | Transmission / %
0.0 | 10
0.2 | 36
0.4 | 54
0.6 | 67
0.8 | 76
1.0 | 82

A sample of a sports drink, treated the same way, gave 76 % transmission.

(a) Describe the relationship between glucose concentration and transmission. [2]
(b) Estimate the glucose concentration of the sample (a sports drink) by interpolation. [2]
(c) Calculate the percentage change in transmission between 0.2 and 1.0 mol dm⁻³. [2]
items.answer: (a) As glucose concentration increases, transmission increases; the increase is not linear and becomes smaller at higher concentrations. (b) about 0.80 mol dm⁻³ (c) +127.8 %
items.markingKey: (a) [2] Positive relationship (A1); non-linear / levels off (A1). (b) [2] Interpolation between the bracketing standards (M1); ≈ 0.80 mol dm⁻³, accept ±0.05 (A1). (c) [2] (82 − 36)/36 × 100 (M1) = +127.8 % (A1).

items.stem: A bar-tailed godwit preparing to migrate from Alaska to New Zealand needs to store 500 kJ of energy. Calculate the mass of triglyceride and the mass of glycogen needed  given that they release 37 kJ g⁻¹ and 17 kJ g⁻¹ respectively. Glycogen is stored with about 2 g of water per gram. Calculate the total stored mass for glycogen and explain the advantage of lipid storage for this animal.
items.answer: triglyceride 13.5 g; glycogen 29.4 g; glycogen + water ≈ 88.2 g; lipid is about 6.53 times lighter, important for mobility
items.markingKey: 500/37 = 13.5 g (A1); 500/17 = 29.4 g (A1). 29.4 × 3 = 88.2 g (A1); lipid stored anhydrous, much less mass to carry (R1).

items.stem: A 1 g sample of a polysaccharide made of 20 glucose units (Mr = 3258) is completely hydrolysed to glucose. Calculate the mass of glucose produced and explain why it is greater than 1 g.
items.answer: 1.10 g; water is added during hydrolysis
items.markingKey: Moles of polymer = 1/3258 (M1); glucose mass = moles × 20 × 180 = 1.10 g (A1); extra mass comes from the 19 water molecules added per polymer (R1).

items.stem: Which group of red cells could safely be given to a patient with blood group B?
items.answer: O or B
items.markingKey: D. B recipients have anti-A antibodies.

items.stem:
Glucose solutions of known concentration were heated with excess Benedict’s reagent for 5 minutes. The brick-red precipitate was filtered off and the percentage transmission of red light through the remaining blue filtrate was measured with a colorimeter.

Glucose concentration / mol dm⁻³ | Transmission / %
0.0 | 13
0.2 | 33
0.4 | 49
0.6 | 60
0.8 | 69
1.0 | 75

A sample of a sports drink, treated the same way, gave 61 % transmission.

(a) Describe the relationship between glucose concentration and transmission. [2]
(b) Estimate the glucose concentration of the sample (a sports drink) by interpolation. [2]
(c) Calculate the percentage change in transmission between 0.2 and 1.0 mol dm⁻³. [2]
(d) Explain why transmission increases as glucose concentration increases. [2]
(e) State two variables that must be controlled. [2]
(f) Suggest why the juice might contain other sugars that this method would not detect. [1]
(g) Outline the advantage of using a colorimeter rather than judging the colour by eye. [1]
items.answer: (a) As glucose concentration increases, transmission increases; the increase is not linear and becomes smaller at higher concentrations. (b) about 0.62 mol dm⁻³ (c) +127.3 % (d) Glucose reduces blue Cu²⁺ ions to brick-red Cu₂O, which is filtered off; more glucose leaves less Cu²⁺ in the filtrate, so it is paler blue, absorbs less red light and transmits more. (e) Volume of Benedict’s reagent and sample; temperature and time of heating; same colorimeter filter/wavelength. (f) Sucrose is a non-reducing sugar and does not react with Benedict’s reagent unless first hydrolysed with acid. (g) It gives a quantitative, objective measurement, so results are more precise and comparable.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] Positive relationship (A1); non-linear / levels off (A1). (b) [2] Interpolation between the bracketing standards (M1); ≈ 0.62 mol dm⁻³, accept ±0.05 (A1). (c) [2] (75 − 33)/33 × 100 (M1) = +127.3 % (A1). (d) [2] Glucose (reducing sugar) reduces Cu²⁺ to Cu₂O (A1); less blue Cu²⁺ remaining so less red light absorbed (R1). (e) [2] Any two (A1 A1). (f) [1] Sucrose non-reducing (A1). (g) [1] Quantitative/objective (A1).
